lines: A revenue-logic bug needs a genuinely long stretch of this shop's own history reprocessed.
The first attempt is one single job, and it runs for most of a day, taking the shared warehouse's own concurrency down for the finance team along the way.
That same job dies right near the end, with absolutely nothing checkpointed anywhere.
That one single job actually failed in three genuinely distinct ways, all at once.
What four decisions, made before the very first chunk ever ran, would have turned this into a completely unremarkable week instead?
answer: Simply reaching for a bigger machine and a longer timeout changes nothing fundamental: that bigger job is still one single unit of work, still dying all at once with nothing saved, and still fighting production for resources, just for a longer stretch now.
Chunking, idempotence, a checkpoint, a throttle, and a shadow table each answer one specific failure this exact job actually hit.

lines: A genuinely long stretch of history gets cut into a grid of chunks, each one covering a day or a partition.
Each one of those chunks is kept fully independent of its own neighbors.
The backfill then advances steadily across that whole grid, one chunk at a time, rather than running as one single undifferentiated job.
A crash stops the backfill cold, somewhere in the middle of its run.
The checkpoint has been quietly tracking every chunk that's already completed, so resuming picks up at the very first incomplete one.
Each chunk overwrites its own output slot in a fully deterministic way, so simply rerunning one never produces a duplicate anywhere.
A concurrency cap and a rate limit on the source reads both exist specifically to leave real headroom for production.
The actual design question here isn't how many workers the budget happens to allow.
It's genuinely what signal should tell this backfill to slow itself down in the first place.
Production's own latency line starts rising, and the concurrency gauge drops in direct, automatic response to it.
Once that latency line falls back down again, the gauge recovers right along with it, completely on its own.
Nobody has to sit there watching it happen.
The backfill's own output fills up a shadow table, sitting quietly beside the live one.
Anyone reading the live table sees absolutely nothing change until one single atomic operation promotes that shadow all at once.
A failed run just gets discarded outright. It's never repaired in place.
Before that swap ever happens, the shadow gets compared against the live table across their overlap.
It also gets checked against an entirely independent recomputation, run on a sample.
That comparison panel has to show only the one change this backfill was actually meant to make, nothing more.
History gets cut into chunks that are genuinely independent of each other.
A checkpoint lets any crash resume safely past the first incomplete one.
A throttle reacts directly to production's own live latency. And a shadow table gets promoted by one atomic swap, gated the whole time by a diff that shows only what was actually meant to change.
One more, to use this for real: a second backfill is already underway, and its own throttle has been switched off by an engineer, specifically to make it finish faster.
Production latency is already climbing, right now, as this happens.
What's genuinely the right move here?
answer: Letting it keep running at full speed treats the throttle as if it were some one-time gate, checked only before the run ever started.
The throttle's entire job is to react continuously to production's own live latency, so re-enabling it immediately lets that same signal govern concurrency again, starting right now.
